label: interactive_input
graph_version: 3.9.8 (3.9.7 + one primary per misconception (S9c) and the four remaining sibling edges (S9b), 2026-11-04; listed in revision_3_9_8)

edges.label:
[0] everyday_reading (E): Novices read a program as if it already knew all its inputs, e.g. treating AREA = HEIGHT*WIDTH written before the input as using the typed values. In fact each read happens only when execution reaches it, and the typed value can change what runs next.
[1] misconception (M) -> InputFixedBeforeRun: wrong rule: All input to a program is fixed before it starts running. Right rule: With StdIn, the user types values while the program runs, and each value can change the control flow. Only command-line arguments are fixed at launch.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> InputFixedBeforeRun: Points to LT (prompt, block for input, test, respond, loop). An uneven trace answers before the guess is read, or reads all the guesses at once. (here mixing in: "All input to a program is fixed before it starts running")

[0] names_the_element (N): Interactive input is user dialogue through standard I/O: the program prints a prompt, reads the user's reply, and its control flow depends on that reply.
[1] states_the_rule (S): A value can be read from standard input at any time during execution, and each read blocks until the user enters input.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Each round prints the prompt, then readInt() blocks until the user types a number and <return>. The value is compared, a response is printed, and the loop test (m != N) runs again.
[1] output_prediction (OP): The terminal shows prompts, typed replies and responses interleaved: What's your guess? 500000 / Too high / What's your guess? 250000 / Too low ... and finally You win!.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One round sets m to the typed value and prints exactly one of You win!, Too low or Too high. N does not change.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Because a StdIn read can run at any point, a read placed inside the game loop lets each reply choose the branch taken in that round.
[1] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: the prompt-read-respond loop (a guessing game or menu). m is a most-recent holder and N a fixed value. The programmer must plan for every possible user reply.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> InputFixedBeforeRun: Redirecting a file of replies instead of typing keeps the same control flow, because the program cannot tell the difference. Only the echo of the typed input disappears from the screen.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use interactive input when later questions depend on earlier answers (games, menus, tutoring dialogues). For bulk data use files and redirection; modern applications take user input through a GUI.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Each reply must be a token of the expected type. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: The user types a non-integer (abc, 12.5) at a readInt() prompt: NumberFormatException.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: No reads after the input ends. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: The user sends end-of-file (<ctrl-d>) before the loop ends, so the next readInt() fails.
wrong: All input to a program is fixed before it starts running. | right: With interactive input the user can change the control flow while the program is executing.
Standard input can be read at any time while the program runs, so the user can type values that change its control flow during execution.
